awd_titl_txt: Travel: NSF Student Travel Grant for 2025 New England Hardware Security Day (NEHWS2025)
awd_abstract_narration:
The New England Hardware Security workshop is a regional, one-day conference designed to bring together hardware security researchers, industry participants, and students in order to develop connections and collaborations between these groups.  This award will fund student participation in the workshop, reducing the financial burden of attending and thus allowing a wide range of junior students from the region to participate. Student attendees will be able to present their work at poster sessions, allowing them to get feedback from a variety of experts.

This award will provide travel support to up to 100 students; the regional nature of the workshop reduces travel costs, accommodating a much wider range of student participants in terms of their career stage and experience in hardware security than most conferences. In particular, the workshop will target early-stage researchers who are not yet attending national conferences, as well as students from disciplinary and personal backgrounds that might not otherwise think to attend a conference on hardware security. This will both increase the chances that participants take up hardware security topics in their future work, grow the hardware research community, and provide participants with ways to connect with potential future employers.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The fifth New England Hardware Security Day (NEHWS) was held on April 18, 2025 at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, MA. The workshop had approximately 180 attendees. Among them were 41 industry participants and representatives from 24 universities. Roughly 30 of the university attendees were faculty members; the rest were primarily students and postdoctoral researchers. In total, 38 attendees identified as female or non-binary. The program included three invited keynotes, two sessions of submitted talks (long and short), a poster session, a panel discussion, and a networking reception. Three presentation awards were given. This NSF award supported student attendance and removed the registration cost barrier for student participants.

Intellectual Merit

The New England region has a strong concentration of expertise in hardware security across universities, industry, and defense laboratories. NEHWS is designed as an industry-and-student centric event to strengthen these regional connections. It rotates among organizing universities and continues to expand participation.

The technical program covered microarchitectural side-channel attacks, fault injection, secure architectures, quantum hardware security, hardware-assisted cryptography, and related topics. These areas are central to building computing systems that remain secure even when adversaries have physical or low-level access to hardware.

Students were active attendees. They gave long and short talks, presented posters, and asked questions during panel discussions led by senior researchers from academia and industry. The format encouraged direct technical exchange. Students received feedback on their research and saw how their work connects to broader system-level security challenges. The presence of industry participants grounded the discussion in practical deployment constraints.

By enabling student participation, the travel grant strengthened the intellectual density of the workshop. Early-stage researchers were able to present work, refine ideas, and engage with a concentrated hardware security community within the region.

Broader Impacts

The primary purpose of this award was to eliminate financial barriers for students. Because NEHWS is a one-day regional event, the main cost to students is registration. Covering that cost allowed broader participation, particularly for students who are early in their research careers or not yet supported by funded projects.

Hardware security is foundational to trust in modern computing infrastructure, including financial systems, healthcare devices, transportation platforms, communication networks, and national defense systems. Training students in this area has long-term societal impact. NEHWS provides exposure to state-of-the-art research, professional development through presentations, and networking opportunities with both academic and industry mentors.

The workshop also strengthens connections among regional research groups. These connections support shared infrastructure, future joint proposals, and sustained collaboration. By supporting student attendance, this NSF travel grant helped maintain and grow a regional ecosystem focused on building secure and trustworthy computing systems.
